correctness.rationale: For any maximum plateau of the uncentered maximal sequence, a maximizing interval cannot cross either lower neighboring value. It is therefore contained in the plateau and has an average equal to the plateau height, forcing contact with the input. Decomposing variation into disjoint peak-to-valley paths proves coefficient 1 for every cutoff. If all intervals are allowed, averaging the entire path between each contact peak and adjacent valley gives factor \(d/(d+1)\) at separation d, bounded by \((n-1)/n\). An endpoint unit impulse attains 1 for every R<n and \((n-1)/n\) for R=n. All endpoint and equality cases are handled. A directly packaged exact-rational checker tested 73,809 ternary profile/horizon cases, 3,000 signed rational cases, and 35 sharpness cases; those tests are corroboration, not the infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The new component is the strict, attained \((n-1)/n\) coefficient on every finite path for all input profiles, and its sharp horizon transition. Earlier real-line and integer-line uncentered theorems establish coefficient 1, not this finite-size sharp improvement. The more recent conjecture of the same numerical coefficient concerns centered graph-ball averages, not all intervals containing the evaluation point. The coefficient-one truncated contraction is compatible with and substantially covered by earlier theory; no separate originality is claimed for that part. Neither inspected primary source nor searches revealed the precise joint classification. A historical equivalent remains possible.

value.rationale: This is the exact attained finite-size constant for a canonical uncentered interval maximal operator, not a numerical table or an arbitrary parameter slice. It identifies a sharp structural threshold at the single largest averaging interval: strict contraction occurs if and only if that interval is admitted. The result refines the coefficient-one infinite-line variation theorem and provides a rigorous full-signal benchmark against a distinct centered finite-path conjecture. Its cutoff boundary is witnessed by a natural endpoint impulse, and all sequence lengths are covered analytically.
